findings.headline: The Council operated within its treasury and prudential indicators in the quarter ended 30 September 2026, and no debt has been repaid or rescheduled in the current year.
findings.detail: The Executive Director of Finance / S151 Officer reports that no difficulties are envisaged for the current or future years in complying with these indicators. The paper also says that no debt repayments or rescheduling have been undertaken to date in 2026/27, although opportunities have increased.
findings.matters: Lenders and other councils look at compliance with prudential limits and whether rescheduling has been used, and the paper reports both.
findings.figures: Operational boundary £35,000k; authorised limit £38,000k; total debt at Q2 £1,126k; CFR £18,949k at Q2
findings.quote: During the quarter ended 30 September 2026 the Council’s has operated within the treasury and prudential indicators set out in the Council’s Treasury Management Strategy Statement.

findings.headline: The Council has £1m of borrowings and has used £17. 949m of cash flow funds in lieu of borrowing, against a capital financing requirement of £18.949m.
findings.detail: The paper describes internal borrowing as prudent and cost-effective in the current economic climate. It says this will need ongoing monitoring if gilt yields remain elevated, particularly in the 25 to 50 year part of the curve.
findings.matters: Using cash in lieu of borrowing keeps the council exposed to a future refinancing need, which lenders and other councils would weigh against current rates.
findings.figures: Borrowings £1m; cash flow funds used in lieu of borrowing £17. 949m (as written); CFR £18.949m; total debt at Q2 £1,126k vs £35,000k operational boundary
findings.quote: The Council has borrowings of £1m and had utilised £17. 949m of cash flow funds in lieu of borrowing as at 30 September 2026.

findings.headline: The Council's new £3m borrowing, budgeted from 1 October 2026 at 3.50%, is hoped to be delayed to January 2027 as one-year PWLB rates are around 5.30%.
findings.detail: The budget assumed new borrowing of £3m from 1 October 2026. The forecast for new PWLB loan interest is £38,334 against an annual budget of £52,500. The paper notes that the balance of external and internal borrowing is driven by market conditions.
findings.matters: A council deferring planned new borrowing because of higher PWLB rates is making a timing decision that other councils and lenders can compare with their own.
findings.figures: New borrowing £3m; budgeted rate 3.50%; one-year PWLB rates around 5.30%; new PWLB loan interest budget £52,500 vs forecast outturn £38,334
findings.quote: It is hoped that this new borrowing can be delayed into January of 2027 but current one year PWLB rates are around 5.30%.

findings.headline: Combined net asset value of the property funds fell by £312,400 in the first half of 2026/27.
findings.detail: The paper reports this as the overall change in combined net asset value across all funds. Cumulative losses since purchase are shown separately, with the Schroder UK Real Estate Fund at £(1,243,475) and the BlackRock UK Property Fund at £(493,062).
findings.matters: Falls in property fund values are a valuation risk for councils holding similar funds, and the paper states that the change is charged to revenue and reversed through the MIRS at year end.
findings.figures: Decrease in combined NAV £312,400 in H1 2026/27; total NAV £13,874,774 vs purchase cost £16,989,766; total loss since purchase £(3,114,992)
findings.quote: The overall change in the combined Net Asset Values for all funds during the first half of 2026/27 has been a decrease of £312,400.

findings.headline: The AEW UK Core Property Fund is in managed winddown, which the paper says is likely to take more than two years.
findings.detail: Shareholders approved the winddown on 31 July 2026. Sale receipts from the fund are expected to start in the current year and will be used to pay the MRP charge, because the original purchase was unfinanced capital expenditure. The M&G UK Property Fund is also liquidating, with distributions of £4,124,317 paid to the Council as of 30 June 2026.
findings.matters: Councils that hold similar property funds bought without borrowing will see whether sale receipts go to MRP, which affects how the funds reduce their capital financing requirement.
findings.figures: AEW purchase cost £4,000,000 and net asset value £3,124,396; M&G distributions £4,124,317 vs £4m original investment; M&G liquidation distributions £241,556 in 2026/27 forecast
findings.quote: The managed winddown of the fund is likely to take more than two years in order to maximise sale receipts.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure at Quarter 2 was £11,054k against a latest revised budget of £31,563k, with an estimated outturn of £31,007k.
findings.detail: The paper links higher cash balances available for investment to slippage in the capital programme. The estimated borrowing requirement for 2026/27 is £7,617k, down from £8,181k in both the approved and latest revised budget.
findings.matters: Capital slippage that leaves cash on hand changes both the borrowing need and the investment income, which other councils and lenders track against forecast spend.
findings.figures: Q2 actual capital expenditure £11,054k; latest revised budget £31,563k; estimated outturn £31,007k; borrowing requirement £7,617k estimated outturn vs £8,181k budget
findings.quote: balances available for investment being higher due to slippage in the capital programme

findings.headline: Net investment income for Quarter 2 shows a favourable variance of £488,971 against budget, with a forecast outturn favourable variance of £490,068.
findings.detail: Net investment income at Quarter 2 was £934,277 against a budget of £445,306. The paper attributes the higher income to market interest rates being above the budgeted return and to higher cash balances from capital programme slippage. Treasury investments achieved an average rate of 4.38% and property funds an estimated 3.21%.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare this with their own investment income, which the paper ties to both higher market rates and capital slippage.
findings.figures: Q2 net investment income £934,277 vs budget £445,306; annual budget £888,180 vs forecast outturn £1,378,248; treasury investments 4.38%; property funds 3.21%; combined 3.83%
findings.quote: On 30 September 2026 there was a favourable variance of £ 488,971 and the forecast outturn was a favourable variance of £490,068.

findings.headline: Auditors record the 2025/26 scale fee at £157,306 plus VAT, compared with £153,022 in 2024/25.
findings.detail: The fee is set by PSAA. The paper also notes non-audit work on Housing Benefit certifications during the year, with safeguards in place to preserve independence.
findings.matters: Scale fee movements are a comparison point for finance officers budgeting external audit costs across councils.

findings.headline: The 2023-24 efficiency programme performance observation is recorded as "Not implemented" by auditors, against a management due date of 31 March 2026.
findings.detail: Auditors recommended a formal programme to identify, RAG-rate and monitor efficiencies, with reporting to a committee and escalation for projects falling behind plan. Management had said officer and member decisions would be recorded from August 2025.
findings.matters: The gap between the due date and the audit status is a concrete example of an efficiency programme slipping, and peers building their own savings tracking can compare the recommended controls.
findings.figures: Management due date 31 March 2026; recorded status "Not implemented"
findings.quote: Status: Not implemented.

findings.headline: Internal Audit gave limited assurance in March 2026 on the identification and monitoring of savings, its second review of that area.
findings.detail: Internal Audit found that governance is now in place to monitor 2026/27 savings, but there is no formally documented escalation process for savings proposals that are not on schedule to be delivered within the year.
findings.matters: A savings-monitoring control that has no documented escalation route for late proposals is the gap that peers facing the same savings targets will be checking for in their own arrangements.
findings.figures: Limited assurance (March 2026); second review of the area
findings.quote: In March 2026, Internal Audit reported limited assurance following its second review of the identification and monitoring of savings.

findings.headline: Auditors have not identified a risk of significant weakness in value for money arrangements across the three domains, and no recommendations to report.
findings.detail: The VfM review covered financial sustainability, governance, and improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness, with no significant risks identified in any domain. Auditors also say they have not identified any performance improvement observations this year.
findings.matters: A clean VfM outcome on financial sustainability is a comparison point for other councils with savings-dependent budgets.
findings.figures: Three VfM domains; no significant risks identified
findings.quote: As noted on the right, we have not identified a risk of a significant weakness in the Council’s arrangements to secure value for money and no recommendations to report.

findings.headline: Unadjusted audit differences have an aggregate surplus impact of £0.2m, which auditors ask the council to adjust for.
findings.detail: The paper says there were no adjusted audit differences that affected the deficit for the year, and that only disclosures were corrected. The unadjusted differences have no effect on the audit opinion, individually or in aggregate.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can see how much unadjusted misstatement a comparable audit carried through to sign-off.
findings.figures: £0.2m aggregated surplus impact; 3.4% of deficit for the year
findings.quote: The aggregated surplus impact of unadjusted audit differences would be £0.2m.

findings.headline: Auditors confirm the LGPS remains in deficit at 31 March 2026, with retirement benefit obligations of £6.7m.
findings.detail: The actuary is re-basing estimate models to the new triennial valuation as at 31 March 2025 for accounting at 31 March 2026. This could correct the defined benefit obligation and asset valuations, and could change contributions and the asset ceiling assessment.
findings.matters: Triennial valuation rebasing can move the pension position in the year it is applied, and councils moving towards surplus face a more complex asset-ceiling test.
findings.figures: £6.7m retirement benefit obligations balance; £3.5m YoY change
findings.quote: We have confirmed the LGPS remains in deficit as at 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: Auditors report controls over journal entries and post-closing adjustments as not effective, because the general ledger does not enforce segregation of duties.
findings.detail: Auditors tested nine high-risk journals and other adjustments, and none were indicative of fraud. The control weakness is structural: the general ledger system does not enforce segregation of duties.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council running a similar ledger system will want to know whether segregation of duties is enforced by the system or by manual controls.
findings.figures: Nine high-risk journals and other adjustments tested
findings.quote: the design and implementation of controls over journal entries and post-closing adjustments were deemed to not be effective.

findings.headline: Auditors report the management review control over land and buildings valuations as "ineffective" under the ISA definition, because there is no counter-signatory to the internal valuer's report.
findings.detail: The internal valuer is the only qualified surveyor used for a significant portion of other land and buildings. Review functions are carried out by finance department staff rather than a second valuer. Auditors say the ISAs make this difficult to design around for estimation uncertainty.
findings.matters: Councils that rely on an in-house valuer with finance-team review face the same control gap in a year when indexation and valuation judgements are increasing.
findings.figures: None stated
findings.quote: Auditing standards require us to report that the design and implementation of the management review control relating to this area is ineffective in line with the ISA definition.

findings.headline: Auditors add a significant risk on indexation of £23.5m of other land and buildings, the first year of the Code change, covering index selection and asset categorisation.
findings.detail: The council adopted a quinquennial revaluation with annual indexation in intervening years. In 2025/26 the Code introduced changes to asset valuation, and auditors found that categorising assets into groups drives the choice of index, so they widened the significant risk to include it.
findings.matters: Other councils moving to indexed valuations under the 2025/26 Code will face the same index-selection and categorisation judgement.
findings.figures: £23.5m indexed other land and buildings; £36.3m other land and buildings balance; +£1.2m YoY change
findings.quote: The total value of other land and buildings subject to indexation was £23.5m.

findings.headline: Auditors expect to issue an unmodified audit report on the 2025/26 accounts, with the audit substantially complete and some outstanding matters still open.
findings.detail: KPMG says it expects to sign its opinion before the backstop date, provided the outstanding matters are resolved. The outstanding items include receipt of the signed management representation letter and finalisation of testing on non-significant accounts. The paper is marked DRAFT.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare the timing and outcome of their own sign-off against a peer that is close to an unmodified opinion before the backstop date.
findings.figures: None stated
findings.quote: We expect to issue an unmodified Auditor’s Report.

findings.headline: Government announces withdrawal of its September 2026 decision to review local government reorganisation, with a review outcome expected in early 2027
findings.detail: The paper records that a July 2026 decision to create a City of Lincoln unitary and a new Lincolnshire unitary was followed by a September review. In October 2026 the government withdrew that review decision, with a structured review now due to report by early 2027.
findings.matters: The shape of local government in Lincolnshire, and the timing of any change, bears on long-term financial planning and on lenders assessing the council's future.
findings.quote: In October 2026 the government announced the above decision has been withdrawn

findings.headline: Register of interests check finds 8 of 10 councillor declarations omitted interests recorded on the council's central register
findings.detail: The auditor reviewed 10 councillor declarations. Eight did not include interests recorded on the council's central Register of Interests and linked to active Companies House roles. A compensating control by PSPS identified these. The auditor records that the interim s151 officer who left in November 2025 did not complete a declaration.
findings.matters: Gaps in declarations of interest, and in the process for leavers, are governance points other councils will check in their own registers.
findings.figures: 8 of 10 declarations reviewed
findings.quote: 8 of the 10 declarations reviewed did not include interests that were recorded on the Council’s central Register of Interests

findings.headline: Interim section 151 officer's turnover during 2025-26 leads to no updated service level agreement with PSPS for 2025-26
findings.detail: The finance function is outsourced to Public Sector Partnership Services Ltd, owned by the three councils in the South & East Lincolnshire Partnership. An updated SLA for 2025-26 was not agreed, mainly due to the turnover of the s151 officer during the year. The 2024-25 SLA remained in place, and the auditor does not consider this a significant weakness.
findings.matters: Changes in s151 officer and the status of an outsourced finance service are issues peer councils with similar arrangements will track.
findings.quote: mainly due to the turnover of the s151 officer during the year

findings.headline: Auditor's Annual Report issued before the 2025-26 financial statements audit is concluded
findings.detail: The auditor states that the report was issued to meet the 30 November deadline. Its work on the financial statements and other information is substantially complete, but no conclusions have yet been reached on those areas. Whole of Government Accounts procedures are also not yet confirmed as complete.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director will want to know that the audit opinion on the 2025-26 accounts is still outstanding and the risk it could still change.
findings.quote: we have not reached our conclusions in respect of these areas

findings.headline: Usable reserves fall from £53.963m to £38.569m between 2024-25 and 2025-26
findings.detail: The key metrics table records usable reserves of £38.569m at 2025-26 year-end against £53.963m the previous year. The paper states that General Fund earmarked reserves fell by £95k, from £17m to £16.95m, and that the council did not rely significantly on reserves to achieve a balanced General Fund position.
findings.matters: A fall in usable reserves of this size, alongside a stated balanced position, is a figure lenders and finance directors will want to understand, since it changes the buffer available for future shortfalls.
findings.figures: £53.963m usable reserves 2024-25; £38.569m usable reserves 2025-26; £17m to £16.95m earmarked reserves; £95k net decrease in earmarked reserves; £2m General Fund balance
findings.quote: Usable reserves 38,569 53,963

findings.headline: Capital budget underspend of £17.1m recorded at year-end against the 2025/26 capital budget
findings.detail: The capital programme approved in March 2025 was £33.3m. The revised budget at 31 December 2025 was £37.4m, and the forecast at that date was £23.6m. The year-end position confirmed an underspend of £17.1m against the capital budget.
findings.matters: A £17.1m slippage against a £37.4m revised budget is a delivery pattern peers and lenders will compare against their own capital programmes.
findings.figures: £33.3m approved capital programme; £37.4m revised budget at 31 December 2025; £23.6m forecast at 31 December 2025; £17.1m underspend
findings.quote: The year-end position confirmed the Council had an underspend of £17.1m against its capital budget for the year.

findings.headline: Medium-Term Financial Plan requires efficiencies of £1.5m in 2027/28, rising to £1.9m in 2030/31
findings.detail: The council has set a balanced 2026/27 budget without additional efficiency savings. The Medium-Term Financial Plan identifies further efficiency requirements each year from 2027/28 to 2030/31.
findings.matters: A balanced current-year budget with a rising multi-year savings requirement is the position many councils will face, and lenders assess whether those savings are identified.
findings.quote: the Medium-Term Financial Plan identifies future efficiency requirements of £1.5m in 2027/28, £1.7m in 2028/29, £1.6m in 2029/30 and £1.9m in 2030/31

findings.headline: Performance improvement observation on a formal efficiency programme remains open after follow-up in October 2025
findings.detail: The auditor first raised a medium-risk observation for 2023/24 that the council had no formal efficiency programme. At follow-up in October 2025 it had not been implemented, and the auditor has kept the recommendation open for 2025/26.
findings.matters: A recommendation carried across two audit cycles is a signal peer councils will track, particularly where efficiency requirements are rising.
findings.quote: we followed-up on this performance improvement observation in October 2025 and confirmed this had not been implemented.

findings.headline: Internal Audit gives Limited Assurance on savings monitoring, with no formal escalation process for savings off schedule
findings.detail: Internal Audit's March 2026 follow-up review gave Limited Assurance on the identification and monitoring of savings. The paper states that a monitoring process exists, but there is no formal escalation route for savings not on schedule. The paper also states that efficiency savings are not separately reported in monitoring reports.
findings.matters: Other councils running efficiency programmes will want to compare how monitoring and escalation of savings is governed, and lenders will look at whether savings slippage would be picked up in time.
findings.quote: there is no formally documented escalation process for any savings proposals that are not on schedule to be delivered within the year.

findings.headline: £0.65m of the 2025/26 efficiency target not delivered by year-end, against a £1.4m target
findings.detail: Of the £1.4m efficiency target for 2025/26, £0.65m was met through Government grant funding. Of the remaining £0.75m, £0.05m was delivered by year-end. The paper states that favourable budget variances offset the shortfall.
findings.matters: Savings shortfalls of this size, with the balance covered by grant and in-year variances, are a question every finance director and lender will ask about recurring budget resilience.
findings.figures: £1.4m efficiency target; £0.65m met through Government grant; £0.75m remaining; £0.05m delivered; £0.65m not delivered
findings.quote: This meant £0.65m of efficiencies were not delivered by the year-end

findings.headline: Boston Borough Council reports a £0.064m underspend for 2025/26, after a forecast deficit of £457k at quarter three
findings.detail: The paper reports the year-end outturn as a small underspend. It records that the quarter three forecast had been a deficit, which the paper describes as not material. The underspend came despite £0.65m of planned efficiencies not being delivered, offset by favourable budget variances including investment income.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council will want to see how a forecast deficit moved to a surplus within one financial year, and what offset the shortfall in savings.
findings.figures: £0.064m underspend; £457k forecast deficit at quarter three; £0.65m efficiencies not delivered
findings.quote: The Council reported an overall underspend of £0.064m for 2025/26,

findings.headline: The paper expects Bank Rate to increase during the remainder of 2026/27
findings.detail: The paper's interest rate outlook for the rest of the financial year is an increase in Bank Rate. The paper gives no quantified forecast in this section.
findings.matters: A forecast rise in Bank Rate affects both the return on the council's cash and the cost of its short-term borrowing, which a finance director at another council will be weighing in the same period.
findings.figures: None given in this section
findings.quote: The expected direction of interest rates for the remainder of the financial year is an increase in Bank Rate.

findings.headline: The combined rate achieved on all investments is 3.83% at Quarter 2, against 3.82% at Quarter 1
findings.detail: The paper reports treasury investments averaging 4.38% (Quarter 1: 4.45%) and property fund investments averaging an estimated 3.21% (Quarter 1: 3.09%). The combined rate is the blended figure across both.
findings.matters: Blended investment returns across treasury and property fund holdings are a benchmark a finance director elsewhere can compare with their own portfolio mix.
findings.figures: Combined rate 3.83% (Q1 3.82%); treasury investments 4.38% (Q1 4.45%); property fund investments 3.21% (Q1 3.09%)
findings.quote: The combined rate achieved on all investments was 3.83% (Q1 3.82%).

findings.headline: M&G Property Fund liquidation distributions of £241,556 are being used to finance an MRP charge
findings.detail: The paper says the liquidation distribution from M&G is included in the Q2 figures and will be used to finance a corresponding MRP charge. The distribution is recorded at Q2 and in the forecast.
findings.matters: Liquidation proceeds from a property fund being applied to MRP is a specific treatment a finance director elsewhere holding similar fund investments may need to plan for.
findings.figures: Liquidation distribution £241,556 at Q2 and in the forecast outturn
findings.quote: The liquidation distribution from M&G which is included in these figures will be used to finance a corresponding MRP charge.

findings.headline: Premature repayment of borrowing produced an HRA discount, with £312,679 allocated in Quarter 2 and £623,650 forecast for the year
findings.detail: The paper records a discount received on the premature repayment of borrowing, allocated in year. It does not name the loan or the lender.
findings.matters: A discount on early repayment of debt is a cost saving a finance director elsewhere can test against their own debt restructuring, and it shows the council repaid borrowing early in 2026/27.
findings.figures: Premiums/discounts allocated in year £312,679 at Q2 and £623,650 forecast for the year
findings.quote: including the HRA discount received on premature repayment of borrowing

findings.headline: The council budgeted to borrow an additional £3m short term from 1 October 2026 at an estimated rate of 3.50%, with current one-year rates around 5.30%
findings.detail: The new borrowing will not be drawn until required. The paper sets the budgeted rate against current one-year rates, which are higher.
findings.matters: A gap between the budgeted short-term borrowing rate and current one-year rates bears directly on the cost of the council's next borrowing, and lenders can see the council is planning to borrow into a higher rate market.
findings.figures: £3m additional short-term borrowing; estimated rate 3.50%; current one-year rates around 5.30%
findings.quote: The Council budgeted to borrow an additional £3m short term from 1 October 2026 at an estimated rate of 3.50%.

findings.headline: Investment balances are higher than budgeted because of slippage in the capital programme
findings.detail: The paper gives slippage in the capital programme as one of two reasons for the higher investment income, the other being market interest rates. The paper does not quantify the slippage in this report.
findings.matters: Capital slippage that leaves cash sitting in investments is a pattern finance officers elsewhere see, and it changes the council's need to borrow in the short term.
findings.figures: None given in this paper
findings.quote: balances available for investment being higher due to slippage in the capital

findings.headline: Net investment income at Quarter 2 is £934,277 against a £445,306 budget, with a full-year forecast of £1,378,248 against a revised budget of £888,180
findings.detail: The paper attributes the higher investment income to market interest rates being above the budgeted return, and to higher balances available for investment. The forecast variance for the year is £490,068 favourable.
findings.matters: Investment income running well above budget is an income source a finance director elsewhere can compare against their own assumptions for market rates and cash balances.
findings.figures: Q2 actual £934,277 against budget £445,306 (variance £488,971); forecast outturn £1,378,248 against revised budget £888,180 (forecast variance £490,068)
findings.quote: The higher level of investment income achieved compared to the original budget is due to interest rates in the market being higher than the budgeted return

findings.headline: Net treasury position at Quarter 2 shows a favourable variance of £730,527, with a forecast 2026/27 outturn favourable variance of £745,790
findings.detail: The paper reports the net treasury position including the HRA discount received on premature repayment of borrowing. The Q2 variance and the full-year forecast are both described as favourable.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare this net treasury outturn against its own budget, and a lender sees the council's treasury result running ahead of budget at mid-year.
findings.figures: Q2 favourable variance £730,527; forecast outturn favourable variance £745,790; Q2 net position (£1,464,396) against budget (£733,869); forecast net position (£2,157,020) against revised budget (£1,411,230)
findings.quote: The net treasury position (including the HRA discount received on premature repayment of borrowing) shows a combined favourable variance of £730,527 and the forecast outturn is a favourable variance of £745,790.

findings.headline: The NNDR Collection Fund shows a £662k deficit at 31 March 2026, shared between the Borough, Lincolnshire County Council and the Government.
findings.detail: The paper also reports a Council Tax Collection Fund deficit of £198k, shared with Lincolnshire County Council and the Police and Crime Commissioner. Both are recorded as balances at year end.
findings.matters: Collection Fund deficits carry into future budgets as a call on the General Fund, which other councils will be watching in their own medium-term plans.
findings.figures: NNDR Collection Fund deficit £0.662m; Council Tax Collection Fund deficit £0.198m
findings.quote: The balance on the NNDR Collection Fund at 31 March 2026 showed a £0.662m deficit.

findings.detail: The paper reports a net increase of £0.044m across reserves. Within that, the Capital Funding Reserve fell by £686k of use, and the Funding Volatility Reserve included the £0.640m 2025/26 surplus.
findings.matters: A net reserve increase after a year of heavy capital drawdown is a position other councils and lenders will weigh against the level of usable reserves.
findings.figures: Net increase £0.044m; total reserves £19,344k at 1 April 2025 to £19,352k at 31 March 2026; Capital Funding Reserve use £(686)k; General Fund £2,000k
findings.quote: The net increase in Specific and General reserves and balances for 2025/26 was £0.044m.

findings.headline: Business Rates income in the General Fund table is £162k above budget.
findings.detail: The table shows Business Rates at £5,225k against a revised budget of £5,063k. The paper does not give the cause in the extracts provided.
findings.matters: Business rates income above budget bears directly on the funding base that other councils rely on under the same retention arrangements.

findings.detail: The General Fund table shows the investment income line at £2,058k against a revised budget of £1,722k. The narrative separately reports income from investment interest of £1.4m.
findings.matters: Investment and property fund income above budget offsets pressure elsewhere, and other councils with similar property holdings will want to see the size of the variance.

findings.headline: Capital outturn for 2025/26 is £20,282k against a revised budget of £37,422k, with the paper attributing the gap to schemes still in progress.
findings.detail: The paper says the capital budget was not fully used because a number of schemes remain in progress, and the funding is needed for completion in the 2026/27 Capital Programme. The largest variances are the Towns Fund Leisure and LUF Crown House schemes.
findings.matters: Slippage of this scale on regeneration schemes is a timing and funding risk that finance officers at other councils managing similar programmes will want to compare.
findings.figures: Grand Total revised budget £37,422k, outturn £20,282k, variance £(17,140)k; Towns Fund - Leisure £7,895k budget against £2,469k outturn; LUF - Crown House £6,025k against £2,951k
findings.quote: The 2025/26 capital budget has not been fully utilised as a number of schemes remain in progress

findings.detail: The 'Efficiencies Required' line carries a revised budget of £(651)k and an outturn shown as a dash, giving a £651k variance. The paper does not explain the line in the sections provided.
findings.matters: An unmet efficiencies target of this size is the type of savings shortfall that other councils' finance officers and lenders track against the medium-term plan.

findings.headline: Boston Borough Council reports a 2025/26 General Fund budget underspend of £64k, with the surplus transferred to reserves.
